source.title: A Study on Overfitting in Deep Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Chiyuan Zhang; O. Vinyals; R. Munos; Samy Bengio

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization and memorization in deep reinforcement learning, extending related questions to maze tasks and reward randomization.
record.gate_note: The study tests A3C agents in generated mazes, including reward-sign randomization, and compares ConvNets with MLPs. Randomized rewards are not natural labels, and the paper does not test the supervised-learning versions about optimizers, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or memorized-example removal.
record.test_reason: The study investigates generalization in A3C maze agents. Its outcomes are episode rewards, not classification errors or accuracies. Random reward memorization is analogous to V1, and the architecture comparison is analogous to V3, but neither measures the behavior those versions specify. No supplied version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that deep RL agents can memorize randomized training mazes while generalizing on regular tasks when model and task biases are compatible. ConvNets outperform MLPs on held-out regular mazes, and greater convolutional capacity improves random-task fitting. They also emphasize that stochasticity can fail to prevent or detect overfitting and recommend isolated training and test sets.
record.recipe_differences: A3C reinforcement learning in generated gridworld mazes with held-out level IDs; compares convolutional and dense architectures, not supervised image classification.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization depends on maze regularity, number of training levels, and architecture. The paper also reports that the effects of random starts and sticky actions vary by task and evaluation protocol.

fits_no_version.finding: On regular BASIC mazes, standard ConvNets achieve test rewards -0.1, 1.2, 2.0, and 2.1 versus MLP rewards -0.6, 0.9, 1.6, and 1.9 at 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 training levels. Big-ConvNet rewards are -0.3, 1.4, 2.0, and 2.1. All reach training reward 2.1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convolutional A3C agents generalize better than fully connected A3C agents on held-out regular mazes with spatially invariant rewards.

fits_no_version.finding: Agents attain near-optimal training rewards on small sets with fixed randomized reward assignments, while held-out performance is poor. Memorization becomes incomplete for larger sets, especially on harder mazes; increased convolutional capacity improves randomized-maze training performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep RL architectures capable of memorizing randomized training tasks can also generalize on regular tasks under the same learning framework.

fits_no_version.finding: Random starts and sticky actions can leave training-environment evaluation scores high for agents with poor held-out performance, and using these perturbations during training does not reliably prevent overfitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic perturbations of training environments do not reliably detect or prevent overfitting in deep RL agents.

record.problems: Results are in a customized gridworld RL environment, not supervised natural-label classification. Architecture tables report averages of top-3 agents selected from 20 runs per setting; uncertainty intervals are not stated. Several randomization and stochasticity results are presented in figures without recoverable numerical values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 report further test rewards at reward-flip probabilities 0.2, 0.4, and 0.5. They are omitted because these random-reward settings do not test V3's natural image-classification condition; the tables show the values in MLP / ConvNet or MLP / Big-ConvNet pairs. Figure-only results for random starts, sticky actions, and learning curves are also not extracted as numerical rows.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and natural-label held-out classification accuracy using the same architecture and training recipe. Reward-sign randomization in RL does not establish these outcomes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error; the architecture pools do not provide this sweep.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification error, the contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, and initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to the supplied versions, despite the study's substantive experiments on RL generalization. The image-like maze observations do not turn policy reward into classification accuracy. Table results average the top three agents selected by training performance from 20 jobs per setting with sampled architectures and hyperparameters; they are not averages over all runs and have no stated uncertainty intervals. Rows with versions ['none'] receive cannot_determine because their measures cannot establish a supplied version, not because their rewards are unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: The study randomizes reward signs in RL rather than fitting fixed random labels and natural labels with the same supervised-learning recipe.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
Uses maze observations and rewards in A3C, not image-classification datasets or the specified fully connected connection-learning and initialization comparisons.
No removal of memorized training examples.
